subtopic: BOUNTY ON BUTTER EXPORTED FROM COMMONWEALTH

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: BOUNTY ON BUTTER EXPORTED FROM COMMONWEALTH
speechtext: Will the Minister of Finance tell me whether any reply has been received from the government of Australia with regard to the reported payment of a bonus of six cents a pound on butter by the stabilization committee in Australia?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOUNTY ON BUTTER EXPORTED FROM COMMONWEALTH
speechtext:
I was just going to send a memorandum to my hon. friend, but since he has asked the question, I will tell him that there is no reply from the government of Australia. Indeed, there is no government subsidy, but I have a telegram from the Canadian Trade Commissioner at Melbourne who advises us that the scheme is purely voluntary, not government controlled. The producers of all states excepting Western Australia and Tasmania have become parties to this arrangement but they are not large producers. The scheme also raises the price to local consumers by three pence per pound above the export London parity; that is they charge their own people three pence per pound more than they charge for export, and the memorandum from the department says that because it is under the Pattersen scheme and a voluntary arrangement they come under our dumping clause and the Customs are so ruling. The Australian agreement provides that the rates thereunder shall be subject to the provisions of the Canadian customs tariff. With reference to the importation of butter into Canada from Australia, if the import price is less than the home consumption value it is liable to the special or dumping duty. The dumping Clause, which is section 6 of the customs tariff, provides in effect that in the case of articles exported to Canada, of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, if the export or actual
The Address-Mr. McGibbon

selling price to an importer in Canada is less than the fair market value in the country whence exported to Canada, there shall, in addition to the duties otherwise established, be levied on such article a special or dumping duty equal to the difference between the export price and the price for home consumption. The special or dumping duty shall not exceed fifteen per cent ad valorem. As the scheme in Australia raises the price to local consumers by three pence a pound above the export London parity, butter from Australia imported into Canada will be subject to the provisions of the dumping clause. The official in my department holds that there will be a dumping duty of approximately fifteen per cent on any butter that enjoys that privilege.

The House resumed from Wednesday, February 24, consideration of the 'motion of Mr. J. C. Elliott for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his Speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed motion of Mr. Bird:	That this
question be now put.

When the House adjourned yesterday I had drawn attention to the amendment of the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird). I pointed out that his amendment

was an infringement on the liberty of the members of this House. I had pointed out also that it either had been moved with the consent of the government or without it; that if it had been with the consent of the government they were hiding behind a cowardly attack which they were unable or had not the courage to make themselves. I had referred to the fact that the government had either been willing or unwilling that the hon. member for Nelson should move this amendment and that if unwilling themselves to move the amendment they were foregoing their prerogative in regard to directing the legislation of this House. In that case I had pointed out that if they no longer were able to command and direct legislation in this chamber, it was their duty to resign.
I wish to point out at this stage something that is very important to the present argument, and that is that we have in power a government who appealed to the people of Canada in October last and who were utterly defeated; that the Prime Minister and eight cabinet ministers were sent to the guillotine, and that in no less than four provinces in this Dominion there is no representation in the goverment. Moreover, they are being kept in power to-day by a party that were not and could not be elected as supporters of this government, and consequently I ask them: By what right do they still linger upon the treasury benches? I had also drawn the attention of the House to the fact that the difficulties confronting this country to-day could be solved by having more work, a greater number of men profitably employed at work in order that they should help to bear the burden of taxation and provide freight for our railways, et cetera, and also greater markets for the products of our farms. Along with this I suggested the necessity of a reduction in taxation and I analysed the consolidated revenue of Canada on a per capita basis showing how much each province was paying. This brings me to the question of the railways which, to my mind, is, with the exception of the war, the greatest problem that ever confronted Canada. Let me repeat what I said yesterday afternoon that the railway question for the east and for the west is one that must receive the consideration of this House. I am one who believes that money will have to be taken out of (he public treasury to help to reduce freight rates from the two extremities of this country, but I wish to register my emphatic protest against the method that has been employed in the past of getting reductions in freight rates. I must congratulate members

The Address-Mr. McGibbon
from the Maritime provinces on the very impartial, judicial and forceful way in which they have presented their case to this country. They have made out an especially good case and I was very much surprised at the reply which the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) made to them. After they had pointed out that they had borne their share in building the Canadian Pacific which did not go into some of the provinces, in building the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific which gave them very little benefit and in constructing the canals of this country from which they also derived very little benefit, when the hon. member for Lisgar got up to reply, he went out into the garbage heap and produced the old argument that he was willing to give them more freedom of trade. They asked for bread and he was not prepared even to give them a placebo.
That brings into review the whole transportation question. We have been developing in this country some three methods of transportation. We have at the present time a western outlet for the prairies. This outlet, as every hon. member knows, has been increasing in value during the last few years and, in my opinion, when the great yellow, brown and black races that are eating less rice and more wheat than ever before, get thoroughly converted to a change of diet, the western route is going to be one of the great exits for our wheat. We have also been developing a system of inland waterways. We have built the Sault canal; we have spent millions upon the Welland canal and, to my mind, all these things are a mistake if we do not carry them to their logical conclusion and make it possible for ocean-going vessels to reach the head of the lakes. The deep waterway system is one which should be continued and pressed to an immediate conclusion. That is all the more important when we consider the large volume of our grain that is going via Buffalo to the Atlantic coast, and it is also important because the power that can ibe developed along that route wili be sufficient to pay interest on the investment.
We have before this parliament a fourth route and .that is the Hudson Bay route which has been put into the Speech from the Throne, as I said yesterday, as a means of seducing and getting support from the western Progressives. While I believe all hon. members on this side will be prepared to look at that problem on its merits, I do not think .they will find very much merit in it when they are finished with it. If I might make a suggestion to the government, it would be that they make a present of this
road, on which we have spent some $14,000,000 in construction and some $6,000,000 in terminals, to the Manitoba and Saskatchewan governments, and throw in three or four million dollars to complete it. I believe this country would be infinitely better off in the end if that suggestion were carried out.
Having prefaced my remarks on the railway question to that extent, I want for the benefit of my good Progressive friends from the west to review the rate question as it pertains to them and to the people of Ontario. On looking up the rate question I find that the rate per ton per mile in western Canada is eighty-seven cents while in eastern Canada it is $1.17. I also find in reviewing returns on grain that were made to this House a year ago, .that the operating costs for 1923 were 126.14 per cent and for 1924, 126.96 per cent, producing an operating loss in the first case of $6,088,499 and in the second, of $5,812,016. Had that same quantity of grain been carried the same distance on United States lines, our western Progressive friends would have had to pay $34,000,000 more in freight than they did. In other words, the farmers of western Canada have an advantage over the farmers of the United States equivalent to $34,000,000 in carrying that quantity of grain that distance. In looking over other returns that were made to this House last year I find that there was a deficit on our railways in the Atlantic region of, roughly speaking, $3,500,000. In the central region there was a net revenue of $16,400,000 while on the United States lines the net revenue was $5,700,000. In the western region there was a deficit of $1,124,000. What are we to deduce from these figures? Simply this, that the central region is carrying the great burden of taxation in connection with the railways so far as freight is concerned, just as I pointed out yesterday that they were carrying also the great burden of taxation in every other direction. I am not objecting to reduced freight rates either in the east or in the west; I want to be perfectly fair and to be well understood in that regard. I said yesterday that the central provinces were quite prepared to share that burden, and I say so again to-day. But I want to register my protest against a system that penalizes *the middle for the 'benefit of the two extremes. I say that this money should be taken boldly out of the treasury for the national good and every citizen in Canada should contribute accordingly to that end.
I was astounded when the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) rose in his place early in the session and charged the government with directly interfering with the
The Address-Mr. McGibbon

railway commission; and I was equally astounded to learn that they had interfered by legislation with railway rates. That is not their prerogative; there should be a freight rate in this country that would allow not only the east and the west but central Canada as well to do business. I submit therefore that the proper method is to take boldly out of the treasury the money that is necessary to recoup the railways for any loss they might suffer in the matter of reduced freight rates. How can we expect the national railways to pay when members in this House advise, and the government act upon that advice, that they be made to carry goods below cost? Day after day we have seen hon. gentlemen getting up in their places and asking the government questions in regard to freight rates, and day after day we have heard the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) agreeing to use his good offices with the Canadian National Railways in the matter. Do we ever hear similar suggestions being made with reference to the Canadian Pacific Railway? Yet the government would have us believe that the Canadian National Railways are out of politics.
For the information of our good Progressive friends let me analyze the railway debt. We have invested in the Canadian National Railways over $2,000,000,000 according to Mr. Bell's report of March 25. On the basis of population Ontario's share of that would be $885,000,000, but if we take as a basis the rates of taxation I have already given its contribution would be two and a half times that sum. We built out of the revenues of the country the National Transcontinental Railway at a cost of $170,000,000 and Ontario's share of that, according to population, was $15,000,000; ' but actually it amounted to $27,000,000. I could go on if necessary and show what proportion of the cost of that railway was paid for by the western provinces, but possibly I have pursued the argument far enough. We have also invested in the canals of Canada $362,000,000 of which Ontario's proportion would be $120,000,000.
On consulting the records of parliament I find that this country has loaned to our western friends through the Seed Grain Relief Act something like $16,300,000 of which the sum of $4,300,000 remains unpaid. I find further that we spent on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police down to 1920 the vast sum of $3o,000,000. I say therefore that when you balance up the accounts between east and west and take the contributions of central Canada into consideration you will find that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec have borne the heaviest part of the burden.

Now we have heard hon. gentlemen getting up day in and day out and telling us how conditions have been improving in Canada. At the same time gentlemen from the extreme east as well as from Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, Winnipeg, Edmonton and the far west have been pleading in this House to have proper freight rates put into force in order to facilitate the movement of coal so that the labourers of these various places may be kept from starvation. So far as the unemployment in these places is concerned, I believe that these gentlemen are right. In the month of January of this year, according to the statistics of this government's own Department of Labour, there were 50,000 people more out of work than there were in the month of December, and this unemployment is widely distributed; it begins at the Atlantic and goes clean across the continent. Every city in every province is faced with more unemployment now than it had to cope with during the month of December. I would direct the attention of the Labour members of this House to a letter written by Mr. Thomas Moore, which contains some interesting statements. It is not necessary for me to explain who or what this gentleman is; he is well known to every member of the House. He is here discussing the situation as it exists here to-day in Canada and the causes thereof, and in relation to unemployment he draws the distinction between a revenue tariff and a protective tariff. He says:
Do Canadian workmen want to make sure of the closing of Canadian factories and of further unemployment? If so they will naturally support a tariff for revenue only.
He then points out that the tariff for revenue as it is applied in England merely taxes the goods they do not produce there such as sugar, fruit and so on, and he ends by saying:
The choice for Canadian workers is between more imported goods and greater unemployment and made in Canada articles and greater oportunities for work at home.
Do the Labour members of this House think that Mr. Moore knows what he is talking about when he says that the very foundation of the Labour market is a protective system?
I also have in my hand the draft of a speech dtelivered by Mr. Stanley Baldwin, Prime Minister of Great Britain, in which he discusses the results of the Safeguarding of Industries Act passed by the Imperial parliament. Let me read to the House the instructions given to the committee by the board of trade regarding the application of the act. The committee were instructed to report on the following:
First, whether the applicant industry-

The Address-Mr. McGibbon
That is, the industry applying for more protection, because that is what it really amounts to.
-is, 'by reason of the volume of employment engaged in the production of the goods to which the application relates, or by reason of the nature of the goods produced, an industry of substantial importance.
Now I want the House to note this:
Second, whether foreign goods of the class or description to which the application relates are being imported into, and retained for consumption in, the United Kingdom in abnormal quantities.
Then follow these further instructions:
Third, whether the foreign goods so imported are being sold or offered for sale in the United Kingdom at prices which are below the prices at which similar goods can be profitably manufactured or produced in the United Kingdom.
Fourth, whether by reason of the severity and extent of such competition employment in the manufacture or production of such goods in the United Kingdom is being, or is likely to be, seriously affected.
Fifth, whether such exceptional competition comes largely from countries where the conditions are so different from those in this country as to render the competition unfair.
Then this note is added by the board of trade :
Com,petition for the purpose of such inquiry is not to be deemed unfair unless it arises from one or more of the following causes,-
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that these causes decidedly apply to Canada to-day.
Depreciation of currency operating so as to create an export bounty.
Is not that the great handicap that the shoe industry, the woollen industry and other of our industries are under to-day?
Subsides, bounties or other artificial advantages.
Is not that the very same thing that the member for iSouth Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) called attention to this afternoon? Is it fair for the dairymen of this country to be subjected to the competition of Australian butter producers not only under the unequal terms of the Australian treaty but under the further disadvantage that their rivals are receiving a bounty of six cents a pound on the butter they export? These are the instructions that were given by the British Board of Trade to those administering the provisions of that special legislation passed to protect the industries and the workingmen of Great Britain.

Mr. Speaker, the
hon. gentleman has indicated the attitude of Mr. Baldwin, the Conservative Prime Minister of England. Would he point out to the House the position taken by Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, leader of the Labour party of Great Britain?

I leave the hon. member to look after his own. I am looking after
the workingmen of my constituency. It is my constituency, as I stated yesterday, that this government by its policy has crucified the labouring men of Canada. The greatest crime that can be charged against any government, Mr. Speaker, is that by its policies it makes it impossible for the people to live in their native land. I contend that this government by its policies has driven out over five hundred thousand of the best workingmen of Canada.

Does the hon.
gentleman contend that the government has done so by heavy reductions of the customs duties?

I say partly yes, partly no. It has brought about these deplorable conditions by putting our workingmen up against the competition of the sweatshops of Europe without any protection. Let me refer a little further to Mr. Baldwin's speech. He analyzes the results so far of the operation of the Safeguarding of Industries Act, and points out-I wish the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) were in his seat to take note of this -that the act has been the means of creating new industries in England. He states what we all know to foe the case, that before and during the war optical instruments, lenses, X-ray equipment and similar goods had to be procured either from Germany or the United States. When I went to the front, Mr. Speaker, I was forced to buy a set of American-German field glasses because they could not be procured either in Canada or Great Britain. Mr. Baldwin points out that the operation of this act has resulted in industries of a scientific nature and very important to Great Britain being established, industries which are now employing tens of thousands of people who otherwise would1 be idle. I would ask the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) if he knows this to be the fact, that when war broke out the great textile industry of England was in jeopardy because it had been relying on Germany for its dyes. The British government spent tens of millions of pounds in scientific industrial research in order to discover the formula for those dyes, and to-day the textile industry is no longer dependent on outside sources.
May I ask another question? Has the hon. gentleman any means whatever of protecting the actual worker in this country against the cheap labour that is being imported from European countries?

Certainly I have. If
the hon. member will only vote with us and
The Address-Mr. McGibbon

turn this government out, we will put in a government that will protect our workers against that cheap labour.
The hon. gentleman is not offering a bribe?

Well, if the hon. member considers any proposal to ensure feeding the wives and children of our workingmen a bribe, I say yes. That is what I am here to accomplish, Mr. Speaker, that is what I am making this speech for-to effect such a change as will bring back the labouring men of my constituency, who have been driven out of their homes and their country by the policies of this government.
Now, Sir, what else has this government done to bring about unemployment? It has raised the cost of the workingman's daily bread higher than it has been for some three or four years, and at the same time it has cut down his wages so that he can hardly make the two balance. I have right in my own constituency-and a similar condition prevails in other constituencies, as the member for North Renfrew (Mr. Cotnam) said recently-men engaged in the hard and laborious lumber industry who are working for twenty-five to thirty dollars a month, and trying to keep their wives and families on those wages. I ask the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre if he thinks he could do so. Clever and all as he is, I will wager that he could not.
Now, what is happening to our labouring men? As I said, half a .million have been driven out by the policies of the government. What would that half a million be worth to Canada to-day if we had them here and a govem-men in power with a policy that would ensure them employment? Five hundred thousand people working at $1,000 a year would mean a lot of money, and that money would be spent in this country, and every man and woman in the country would derive a certain amount of benefit from its expenditure. That would help to solve our national railway problem, to a (certain extent, at least; it would help to pay the national debt of this country, and help us to bear the great burden of taxation that is driving the people of this country almost into the earth. While on this subject I might quote the ex-Minister of Finance, the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton),, who a year ago made the statement in this House that there was being brought into this country $700,000,000 worth of goods which we had the machinery and the workmen here to (make ourselves. Let us analyze that for a moment. When I say that labour accounts for 70 per cent of

the cost of (the manufactured article, I think I am well within the mark. Now 70 per cent of $700,000,000 is $490,000,000; $490,000,000 would pay $1,000 a year to 490,000 men; it would give employment to nearly half a million men, and we could provide that work for them if we would only do what any patriotic, reliant, self-respecting people ought to do, give employment ito our own people by making the goods we need at home.
Now I want to leave the labouring man for a moment and go to some other parts of my constituency-but no, I will finish him up while I am at it. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), if he will go back to his constituency and laugh at those who are trying to get bread for the labouring men of this country, is not worthy to represent them in this House. I have in my hand a brief analysis of the shoe industry in this country, and I take this up because it relates to industries that are located in my riding, industries which are more or less dependent on the shoe and leather industry in this country. I want to bring to the attention of the House this fact, that this government has lowered the duty on boots and shoes to such an extent, and by treaties and other means has so wiped out the protection we had against the depreciated currencies of other countries, that our own industries can hardly live. He thus earns a living while helping to develop the country. As a student of technical education he helps scientific research. Let us take for example a young student like Dr. Banting and think of all he did for humanity and civilization just by studying and working in a laboratory. He started in a very small way and he often met discouragement, as every poor student does. If we should take a leaf out of the book of Germany for a national policy in regard to our students and, instead of letting them in the summer time work at such menial jobs as cooks and waiters and in other poorly paid positions of that kind, we should secure some of them for four or five months to help in the development of our resources, and the carrying on of national research. We would thus be doing something to develop Canada for the benefit of future generations.

Yesterday the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) made some reference to the diversion of water at Chicago, and here again the government is betraying an utter inability to cope with the situation. This is a most important matter for the lake towns and the ports on the Great Lakes. It has been estimated by the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario that there has been an annual loss to Canada as a result of this diversion of water from the lakes of $35,000,000 a year and I am bound to say that I am not at all satisfied with mere protests on the part of the government. The Americans never pay any attention to such protests; they will continue to ignore them. This treaty was solemnly entered into between two nations, Great Britain and the United States, and Canada is not even a party to it. The International Deep Waterways Commission acts a3 intermediary between the two countries in the observance of the treaty, and in this connection I would point out, in reference to the question which was put by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) yesterday, that the Secretary for War in the United States has no power in the matter. He is a ministerial official, his positidn being analogous to that of the Minister of Public Works in this country. The harbours and the Great Lakes are under his control and all expenditures for public works are made under his direction. He is not mentioned in the treaty nor is Chicago a party to it. The amount of water to be taken from the lakes for given purposes is clearly set out in the treaty, so much for Canada and so much for the United States, and not only are they taking the allotted 10,000 feet in Chicago but they are now drawing off as much as 16,000 feet. And in addition to that they are securing from the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario 10,000 or 12,000 feet on a contract which has still four or five years to run.
Now what I object to particularly in this matter is the fact that private citizens of this country are going to Washington and interviewing the President of the United States in regard to the treaty. I consider it a piece of impertinence for any private citizen of Canada or any private organization here to wait upon the United States authorities, going over the head of the British government, the Canadian government and the British

Embassy at Washington and. ignoring the Canadian government without even making representations to the minister or government here. yearly, and what that department does I confess I do not know. What, for example, has it done in connection with this very subject I have been discussing, the diversion of water at Chicago? In the session of 1922 I introduced a resolution for the adoption of a national coal policy, so that every pound of coal used by Canada would be mined and coked under the British flag. At the time I was laughed at by certain hon. members and by some of our newspapers for what they termed the ridiculous policy of attempting to displace Pennsylvania coal in the central provinces. But I have lived to see my policy endorsed by the country. Our people now realize that the American mine owners could freeze us out in one winter. I was surprised to hear my hon. friend from Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) say last night that he does not burn Alberta coal but likes Pennsylvania. Well, Toronto wants to bum Alberta coal. So far as I am concerned, this national fuel policy is not going to be laughed out of court by Sir Henry Thornton or anybody else. Would it not be far better for us to adopt the British policy and so put this important Canadian industry on its feet, and at the same time make ourselves independent of the United States for our fuel supply? We should protect our industries -agricultural, manufacturing and mining-and we should also protect our workmen from all evil effects of dumping. Financial Reorganization
In his commentary on the year's operations, Sir Henry Thornton, president and chairman of the National Railway board, again refers to the allimportant question of capitalization, and reports that active consideration is being given to the policy to be followed in connection therewith "and the extent to which, if at all, advances made and capital held by the government should be written down to a figure commensurate with the earning prospects of the property." The president and chairman adds that the problem is proving both difficult and complicated, but it is hoped shortly to be able to present to the proper authorities a consistent scheme for consideration.
This question of financial reorganization of the Canadian National system is one of the most pressing problems that to-day confront the management and the government. The greater part of the Canadian National mileage was formerly privately owned. Due to over-expansion and to conditions due to the war, these railways found it impossible to carry on and were taken over by the government. Had the railways been obliged to liquidate their affairs, readjustment of capital charges would have taken place at that point. Less drastic methods resulted in the transfer of these railway properties to the government of Canada, and with them the heavy capital charges which private ownership had found it impossible to carry.
The next paragraph in the report refers to the funded debt of the National railways. One-half of this funded debt consists of guarantees and loans by the government of Canada and the other half is money lent by private people. The part advanced by the government does not pay dividends; it is a frozen asset. The other part does pay dividends. I want hon. members to listen to these two paragraphs because they constitute the whole key of the transportation problem as affecting the National Railways: The Funded Debt
The long-term funded debt of the Canadian National Railways is given in the balance sheet as $2,050,181,517.70. Of this sum $913,913,082 was supplied by the investing public, and two-thirds of this debt due the public is guaranteed by the Dominion, of which it is, therefore, a contingent liability.
Forming part of the long-term funded debt are advances totalling $560,397,957.64 by the Dominion government to railways now included in the National
system. On this immense sum interest amounting to $130,157,922.28 has accrued. This the railways have not been able to pay, and accrued interest has been added to principal, though in such cases it is not compounded. Thus the total advances, including interest, now amounting to $690,555,949.92, as indicated in the balance sheet.
Included in the $2,056,181,517.70 given as the sum of its long-term funded debt in the balance sheet is an item of $451,712,484.98, which represents the amount Canada has spent in the construction, maintenance and operation of former Canadian Government railways, such as the Intercolonial, the Prince Edward Island railway, eastern branch lines and the Transcontinental, the eastern division of the projected Grand Trunk Pacific.	It has not been the practice to
reckon interest on these advances to the original Canadian Government railways, so that the item referred to is exclusive of interest. The inclusion of these advances on appropriation account, Canadian Government Railways, among the liabilities of the Canadian National lines is entirely a bookkeeping requirement rendered necessary by the fact that a corresponding item is included among the investments in road and equipment on the asset side of the ledger. It is well, however, to point out that this item of $451,712,484.98 is not a liability of the Canadian National railways, though it is money which the Dominion has put into railways apart altogether from the properties taken over by reason of the failure of private ownership.
Interest Charges
The question of interest has been referred to. Owing to the varying practices in the financial operations of the respective systems which make up the Canadian National lines, this question of interest of itself presents difficulties when the possibility of uniform financial practice is being considered. As already stated, no interest is reckoned on appropriations to former Canadian Government railways, for the construction of which there were no public borrowings. Nor is interest accrued on the amount due the government for unpaid interest on loans and advances, which amounted to $130,157,992.28 on December 31, 1924. The above sum represents simple interest on the $560,397,957.64 advanced by the government to former privately-owmed roads. In 1924 alone the accrued interest on this account amounted to $31,271,043. Five years ago the corresponding item was $14,346 831.69.
Interest due the public cannot be deferred as is interest due the government.
You cannot defer interest due to the public in the way you can stand the government off and compound the interest. You have to pay the investing public interest on their investment.
If not earned it must be borrowed; and, if borrowed from the public, interest on such amount is compounding from year to year. Last year (1924) fixed charges due the public amounted to $38,361,704.14; for 1920 the corresponding item was $31,055,318.28. Interest charges due the government and the public combined, which amounted to $45,402,149.97 in 1920, had grown to $69,632,747.14 in 1924. Including the Central Vermont, the total interest charges last year were $70,759,016.23. The rapid growth of interest charges emphasizes the importance of the examination of the capital structure of the Canadian National railways to which Sir Henry Thornton has referred.

The debt of Nova Scotia has been multiplied by ten during the last twenty-five years. In 1900 its liabilities amounted to $4,059,517, but on September 30, 1925 they had reached a total of $40,130,119. In 1900 the funded debt of the province was $3,776,033 and in 1925 it was $35,267,927. That progress has been accelerated during the last three years. From 1922 to 1925 we have gone in debt in Nova Scotia at the rate of $5,000,000 a year. The debt of a province is not a very serious thing if the value of its assets continues to advance proportionately. But such is not the case in Nova Scotia. We find our debt increasing, we find our assets diminishing and our sources of wealth growing less year by year. Our revenue in the province is chiefly derived from our coal. In 1921 we produced about 5,734,928 tons of coal. In 1923 the production amounted to 6,597,838 tons, and in 1925 it dropped to 3,842,166 tons. I do not for one think that confederation is the sole cause of our present problems in Nova Scotia, but confederation, the union of Nova Scotia with the rest of Canada, let loose in that province certain economic forces that are largely responsible for those problems. The two provinces of Quebec and Ontario were very much larger and wealthier than the little province of Nova Scotia. Very shortly ' after confederation the competition from those upper provinces wiped out the industries of the lower provinces, and the wholesale offices and business concerns of the upper provinces very speedily put out of existence all the commercial houses of Nova Scotia. To-day you have in the Maritime provinces a market of a million people, practically controlled by the two provinces of Quebec and Ontario. Surely it is worth while for Quebec and Ontario to make some sacrifice in order to retain that market, and that sacrifice we are going to ask them to make.
Certain other results followed from that union, possibly the most important of all being the draining of the financial resources of Nova Scotia to the central provinces of Quebec and Ontario. Twenty-five years ago we had in Nova Scotia half a dozen banks- small ones, it is true, but each serving certain business interests in a restricted area. The bankers of those days were like country dealers; they knew all the resources of their customers, whose friends they were, and they were able to advise their customers on all matters of interest to them. But what has happened? To-day we have not one bank in Nova Scotia. All our banks have been merged, gobbled up, and their headquarters

The result of this-and I venture to say it is largely the cause of the agitation for Maritime rights- was disclosed when a year or two ago an attempt was made by various municipalities to make those banks pay a fair rate of taxation. It was then learned that all the savings deposits in those banks were transferred to headquarters in Montreal or Toronto and invested from there. In that way practically all the financial resources of Nova Scotia have been drained out of that province and are managed to-day from Montreal or Toronto by this small number of wealthy men who, it is alleged, control all the financial interests of Canada. I have no doubt hon. members have received this extract which I hold in my hand from an address delivered by the general manager of the Royal Bank of Canada at its annual meeting in which he paid particular attention to this idea and set forth the benefits to Canada of having big banks with branches spread throughout the country. That may be all right in theory, but in practice it has been fatal to Nova Scotia.
Following our money went our industries. The greatest industry we have to-day in eastern Canada is the British Empire Steel Corporation, and it should be a purely local concern. It was started in 1893 when all the little mines in the county of Cape Breton were merged in the Dominion Coal Company. From that a still larger merger was effected in the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, and two or three years ago the British Empire Steel Corporation was formed, the headquarters of that institution being moved to the city of Montreal. The result is that we have the principle of absentee landlordism in our greatest industry in the east. We have had trouble recurring every year. Why? Because the executive of that corporation are a thousand miles away from the men who earn their money for them. We think if we had a local executive rubbing shoulders with the men and entering into their interests, a great deal of the cause of all this trouble would be wiped out. I had as one of my opponents in the last election the labour leader, Mr. James B. McLachlin, who contested that constituency on no other ground than opposition to the Besco.
